line: Anil Bhatt. Accountant. I do the free tax help here in February and coach Little League in April. In between, I tell people to stop worrying.
Whether their kids are losing Gujarati. Mine never had it. Neil and Priya. My kids won't need any of this, and that's fine. Neil is pitching varsity.
choice1: Do you miss it for them?

line: I came in 1991 for an MBA with two suitcases. I learned the accent, the handshake, the weather small talk. My kids got all that for free. That's the gift.
My mother thinks I gave something away. Maybe. She also asks Neil to do her taxes. In English. I don't hear her complaining about that part.
Little League signups. Twelve kids, three named Aarav. I gave them numbers. The kids are happy. Their mothers are less happy.
Quarterly audit. Your finance people keep receipts in a shoebox. I'm not judging. I'm a little judging.
Advice I gave my nephew: on LinkedIn, use the short name. 'Vik' gets callbacks. 'Vikramaditya' gets 'we'll be in touch.' It's not fair. It's true.
choice2: I'd rather they learn the name.

line: Little League pancake breakfast, Sunday, at the Rotary hall. All the parents, one griddle, terrible syrup. Come. You'll meet half the useful people in town.
Clients ask me if filing taxes puts them on a list. I tell them: file. A clean record is the best protection. Be boring on paper.
Tax forms in Hindi and Gujarati now. My mother is thrilled. I'm thinking: now nobody will learn to read the English one.
Every time I come, you're here. Good people, good chai. But don't let Deshpande turn you into a committee. The city is bigger than this hall.
A friend at your office says you're doing well. Good. Show up, do the work, and after a while nobody asks where you're from.
Anil gives you a polite, short smile.
